#10532. American Express just made one of its most popular credit card perks even better

American Express is giving cardholders another reason to make their dinner reservations through Resy.

The company is launching Resy Rewards Tuesday, a new loyalty program that lets eligible Amex cardholders earn four additional Membership Rewards points per dollar they spend at participating restaurants. Those points are in addition to whatever rewards their credit card already earns, so that means some diners could earn as much as 8X points on a single meal.

The program marks the first time American Express has brought its Membership Rewards program directly into the Resy app, bringing together two of the company’s biggest offerings as competition for restaurant loyalty heats up.

How Resy Rewards works

Resy Rewards will initially be available in New York City, with plans to expand to additional U.S. markets in 2027.

Eligible American Express cardholders can enroll their cards in the program through the Resy iOS app (Android support is coming soon). Once enrolled, you’ll find a new Rewards tab where you can browse participating restaurants and make reservations.

To earn the bonus points, diners need to book through that Rewards tab, complete their reservation, and pay for their meal using their enrolled American Express card.

They’ll then earn four additional Membership Rewards points for every eligible dollar spent, on top of the points their card would normally earn.

For American Express Gold Card members, for instance, who already earn 4X points on qualifying restaurant purchases, that means earning up to 8X points per dollar spent. That means a $200 dinner that would normally earn 800 points could earn 1,600 points through Resy Rewards.

Eligible American Express Business Gold Card members can also earn the additional points. However, the card’s existing 4X restaurant rewards depend on restaurant spending being among the cardholder’s top two eligible spending categories during the billing cycle. A points cap also applies.

At launch, Resy Rewards will be available at a selection of New York City restaurants, including Carne Mare, Colonia Verde, Hearth, Kiko, OPTO and Le Pavillon.

The company plans to expand the program to additional U.S. cities in 2027, when select restaurants on Tock, another reservation platform owned by American Express, will also become eligible to participate.

Why American Express is betting on restaurant rewards

Restaurant loyalty has traditionally been a difficult business. Diners want flexibility in where they eat, while restaurants need to balance the cost of offering incentives against the additional business those programs generate.

American Express has an advantage because it doesn’t need to create an entirely new rewards system. Instead, Resy Rewards uses Membership Rewards, an established points currency that millions of American Express cardholders already collect through everyday purchases.

“For the first time, we’re bringing American Express’s industry-leading Rewards program into the Resy iOS app and connecting two things our Card Members value deeply: great dining experiences and meaningful rewards,” said Pablo Rivero, CEO of Resy and senior vice president of American Express Global Dining.

“As we’ve seen with the success of the Resy Credit, rewarding diners while driving demand and revenue to Resy restaurants is a win on both sides of the table.”

American Express points to the success of its existing Resy Credit as evidence that dining incentives can influence consumer spending. According to the company, spending on Resy Credit-eligible American Express card products increased 33% at U.S. Resy restaurants following the credit’s introduction. The credit has also been redeemed at 98% of U.S. Resy restaurants.

For most developers and freelancers, all of it lives in Google Workspace or Microsoft 365. Both are excellent tools, and both encrypt your data in transit and at rest. But in their standard setup, the provider holds the encryption keys, which means your provider (and the integrated apps and AI features connected to it) can access what's inside.

Proton Workspace takes a different approach: the same everyday tools, with encryption designed so that not even Proton can read your data.

Here's how the three compare, what each does best, and which makes the most sense for how you work.

Google and Microsoft are built around ecosystem integration. Proton is built around keeping your data yours, without sacrificing productivity tools.

#10530. Lab-grown chicken is finally becoming affordable. Will consumers bite?

There’s something new on the menu at Epic Steak, an upscale restaurant across the street from Google in San Francisco: “Cultivated” chicken, made partly from chicken cells grown in bioreactors, is now offered to diners right alongside staples like porterhouse and Wagyu.

Epic is one of eight California restaurants that serves the food, along with some corporate and college campuses, including Stanford University. The Bay Area startup behind the cultivated chicken, Upside Foods, says it has reached a new milestone in scaling up its production—and that has helped bring the price down in the range of premium farm-raised chicken. Its new product includes a blend of cultivated chicken and plant-based ingredients like soy and olive oil.

At Epic, “Southern Fried Upside Chicken” with kimchi slaw and hot honey aioli sells for $12. Waterbar, a neighboring seafood spot with the same chef as owner, sells a five-spice version of Upside chicken for $15. At Chimmelier and Jilli, popular Korean fried chicken restaurants in Los Angeles and San Francisco, K-Pop Chicken made from the new meat sells for $19.

“We can put it at a price point on the menu where it can be available for everybody,” says Parke Ulrich, executive chef and owner at Epic and Waterbar. Two of his other Bay Area restaurants, Mersea and Hurrica, will also serve dishes made with Upside chicken.

Upside, which launched in 2015 and has raised around $600 million, has spent years on R&D for its cultivated meat—meat produced without raising animals or using slaughterhouses, using real animal cells that grow in tanks the company calls cultivators.

The company was originally called Memphis Meats, but rebranded in 2021 with a name that it saw as more consumer-friendly. It’s one of more than 140 companies working in the space of cultivated meat. A handful are selling products on the market, including Vow, which sells cultivated quail and fois gras in Australia, and Wildtype, which sells cultivated salmon at a few U.S. restaurants.

In theory, producing meat this way could help reduce the enormous environmental footprint of animal agriculture, though that depends on how it’s made, including how much energy is used.

The space has been slow to take off, and some other companies have faced difficulties. Good Meat, another Bay Area-based cultivated meat brand, stopped commercial production in the U.S. in 2024. Two other startups, Meatable and Believer Foods, folded late last year.

Over the last several years, “the biggest challenge was the external skepticism that this would have worked,” says Dr. Uma Valeti, cofounder and CEO of Upside Foods. The company first unveiled a commercial facility in 2021, though it didn’t initially use its large-scale bioreactors. (Wired reported that it struggled to use the equipment; the company says that its early R&D challenges have been fully addressed.)

In 2022, when the company got regulatory approval of an earlier version of its chicken, it was produced at a small scale. Customers had to make reservations for the dish, available only in limited quantities, at a restaurant that sold it temporarily, or find it at one-off events.

Now the company says large-scale production is underway. Upside has built a much larger production line, with 20,000-liter tanks in addition to its earlier equipment. Valeti says the two-story-tall tanks “are the largest of their kind in the world,” including anything ever used in the pharmaceutical industry. (The company had previously planned to build a factory in Illinois, but retrofitted its Emeryville headquarters with the giant equipment instead.)

In a year, it claims that it has the capacity to produce more than a million pounds of Upside Chicken on less than half an acre of land. One cultivator produces 1,500 to 2,000 pounds of meat a day; the next “harvest” will begin later this week. Inspectors from the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the Food and Drug Administration work on-site, using a new regulatory process that was developed for this type of food.

Scale helps bring down cost. The company makes a key ingredient for its cell feed, something that was expensive to source previously. The chicken itself has also been redeveloped and now includes some plant-based ingredients. That helps improve the texture and nutrition of the food, Valeti says, but also reduces cost. The company declined to comment on the percentage of the food that’s made from cultivated chicken cells versus plant-based ingredients, saying only that cultivated chicken is the second ingredient after water.

For restaurants and cafeterias, the chicken comes in whole cuts, cubed, or shredded varieties. Ulrich, who has been developing recipes for his restaurants with Upside Foods over the last several months—experimenting with everything from soup to a barbecue chicken sandwich—says the chicken flavor is subtle, since the product is a blend. But the texture is “fantastic,” he says. It “peels apart like a chicken breast would. It has those strands. And it’s just very silky in texture.”

Upside wants to show demand at the restaurants and cafeterias it works with now, and then will scale up production more and potentially begin retail sales. With more scale, and production facilities built outside the expensive Bay Area, the cost will come down even further.

The big question: How many consumers will be willing to eat it? The market for alternative meat has been struggling for a few years. Plant-based meat sales in the U.S. are roughly half of what they were in 2021. As consumers increasingly look for “clean” ingredients—simple, recognizable, and natural—cultivated meat’s production methods are a harder sell. Even as the taste gets closer to conventional chicken, the food is still likely to be perceived as different.

Texture is key, chef Ulrich says: “My focus has been trying to get the texture there, because I think people eat with their eyes, and it’s almost more important sometimes than how they taste it. Because if it doesn’t look like chicken, if the look isn’t there, their taste buds automatically go somewhere else.”

After rumors of Nvidia GeForce RTX 5090 graphics cards being withdrawn from the consumer retail channel, it is pleasing to see major U.S. e-tailers like Newegg stuffed with stock today. Checking out this popular online electronics retailer, we note that there are 21 RTX 5090 SKUs available, and 11 are sold by and shipped by Newegg. Sadly, pricing remains in 3x MSRP+ territory at the time of writing. Remember, you can sift through pricing trends in our comprehensive GPU price tracking 2026 feature to see that Nvidia's Blackwell flagship was once available at its fabled sub-$2,000 price.

Despite what looks on the surface like an ample supply (but there are order limits of one per customer), prices for RTX 5090s remain extremely high. The best prices we can see at Newegg are $6,599, but this price applies only to a water-cooled Aorus model and another sold inside a Gigabyte AI BOX eGPU. They might still appeal to you, depending on your setup, though.

For a ‘standard’ air-cooled graphics card, albeit a very nice Aorus RTX 5090 Master, you’ll need to squeeze at least $6,659 out of your savings. A bonus with this card, alongside several others from the Gigabyte stables now purchasable from Newegg, is that it comes with a free motherboard. Many of these Gigabyte Aorus designs are being bundled with a full-ATX-sized X870 Aorus Elite WIFI7 AM5 motherboard, purportedly worth $319. Please note that the same motherboard is available to purchase outside this bundle for a more reasonable $249.

If you have money to burn, there are plenty of even more expensive SKUs to pick from. There are no opulent Golden Dhabab models on Newegg, sadly, but you’ll still be asked to part with $11,896 for the Asus ROG Astral GeForce RTX 5090 Edition 20 (sold by a Newegg marketplace partner). Perhaps surprisingly, given recent trending pricing news, that’s the only model above $10K, but there are still many models that are almost $10,000 from Asus, MSI, and Zotac. Even an Nvidia Founders Edition RTX 5090 refurb is priced at $8,899.

In context, these RTX 5090s are still at astronomical prices for consumer gaming PC add-in hardware. But they are now purchasable from a big retailer with fast delivery, rather than off a random scalper. It was only a month ago that rumors swirled about the RTX 5090 and the RTX 5080 being withdrawn from retail. That seemed to trigger crazy levels of price inflation, and reports of $10,000+ prices for the flagship card seemed to become the norm.

One can only hope that stock continues to flow to Newegg and other outlets, and RTX 5090 / RTX 5080 prices will settle lower as a result.

#10527. Networking is awkward: Marriott and Second City want to improve your conference experience with improv

Corporate networking hours can be painfully awkward. Picture it: dozens of professionals clutching lukewarm drinks, trading similar elevator pitches, and desperately scanning badges to find someone worth talking to.

“You have a name tag, a drink in your hand, and no guidance,” Tyler Dean Kempf, creative director of Second City Works, told Fast Company. “It’s up to you to engage people in conversations that are usually focused entirely on work.”

Marriott International thinks it has a fix—and it involves pulling a move straight out of the comedy playbook.

On Tuesday, the hotel giant announced Unscripted Networking: The Second City Takeover, a new program developed exclusively with Chicago’s 65-year-old improv comedy institution, the Second City.

The program is rolling out across more than 125 properties in Marriott Bonvoy’s Convention & Resort Network throughout North America and the Caribbean. It offers a 45- to 60-minute experience that swaps traditional small talk for structured, improv-inspired group play.

A different kind of workplace networking event

Rather than putting individuals on the spot for solo stand-up bits, the program pairs two professional Second City hosts with a live music director who formats the session like an interactive variety show.

The events are designed for groups of 50 to 750 attendees; the hosts lead rapid-fire transitions through low-stakes exercises by asking participants to debate topics like coffee versus tea, or window versus aisle seats, rather than their resume highlights.

In one drill, Kempf noted, attendees act as “corporate wingmen,” learning about a partner before introducing them to another pair in the room to expand their circle.

Kempf emphasized that while pitching improv to corporate professionals might send introverts running for the exit, the structure explicitly removes the fear of performance.

“When we say the word improv, people get scared because our minds go to being vulnerable, having no script, or performing on stage,” Kempf said. “There’s no performance in this. Our hosts demonstrate vulnerability first from the stage, which signals that it’s safe for people to drop their guard down on the floor.”

Let’s get together

Amanda Cox, vice president of Sales, Convention & Resort Hotels, East Region for Marriott International, said as hybrid work environments reduce daily office interactions, live events are bearing an unprecedented burden.

“In recent years, there’s less gathering around the proverbial water cooler,” Cox said. “Live meetings and events are being looked upon to be torchbearers of an organization’s culture—and that’s a lot of pressure on event planners.”

That pressure is compounded by the challenge of bringing together a multi-generational workforce with different communication norms.

Cox noted that in customer insight sessions with event organizers, Marriott found planners struggling to get younger hires and veteran executives on the same page. 

“It is amazing the barriers that break down when you’re immediately in a place of creative collaboration,” Cox said.

Yes, and…

Marriott ran nine internal engagements with Second City over the past year to test the concept before scaling it across its resort portfolio.

Cox said that incorporating the program at the opening reception of a typical three-day conference can result in deeper engagement throughout the rest of the event.

“When you start with that genuine connection, you see the return on investment grow throughout the entire meeting,” Cox said. “You’re getting deeper much quicker because you’ve stepped away from small talk into substantial connection.”

By bringing comedy-backed behavioral science into the ballroom, Marriott and Second City are making a clear bet: The fastest way to get corporate professionals to drop their guard isn’t another open bar—it’s getting them to play along.

The CS 737X CDU (v2) brings an authentic, premium-build Boeing 737 Control Display Unit to the home cockpit, but its high price makes it a niche product for serious flight sim enthusiasts.

Accurate 1:1 replica of the real Boeing 737 Control Display Unit

Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Thanks to the popularity of Microsoft Flight Simulator 2020, followed by Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, a growing number of companies have entered the flight simulation peripheral market — offering everything from budget-friendly products to high-end equipment designed for professional and home cockpits.

Cockpit-Master and Cockpit-Simulator were jointly founded in 2018 to develop and manufacture flight simulation equipment. In 2024, the company was split into two divisions, with Cockpit-Simulator focusing on more premium, professional-grade equipment.

Today, we are looking at the CS 737X CDU v2, a 1:1 replica of the Boeing 737 Control Display Unit (CDU). We will examine its build quality, how closely it replicates the real 737 CDU, and how well it integrates with Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024.

Before taking a look at the product itself, let’s first look at the real 737 Control Display Unit (CDU) and explain its functionality.

The CDU is the primary interface pilots use to interact with the aircraft’s Flight Management System (FMS). The FMS can be thought of as the aircraft’s “brain,” handling a wide range of navigation and performance-related tasks. Pilots use the CDU to enter and modify the flight plan, while the FMS calculates the lateral route and vertical profile of the flight. It also manages performance calculations, monitors fuel and flight progress, and provides guidance to the autopilot.

The CDU features a display screen with six line select keys on either side. These keys allow pilots to select and enter information into specific fields on the display, including data entered into the scratchpad. The CDU also includes dedicated function keys for tasks such as accessing performance information and entering instrument departures and approaches. Below the display is an alphanumeric keypad, which pilots use to enter text and other data before transferring it to the selected field using the line select keys.

Unlike other consumer grade CDUs on the market, the CS 737X CDU v2 uses a full-metal, CNC-machined aluminum shell.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The buttons are made of silicone rubber, which also closely replicates what we felt in our time on a 737 simulator.

The display is where we noticed the biggest departure from the real 737 CDU. The real unit uses a thick, chemically strengthened, anti-glare optical glass cover, whereas the CS 737X CDU v2 uses a standard commercial display. As a result, there is some glare, although the display itself is excellent and offers very wide viewing angles. Despite this difference, the visual presentation is remarkably close to that of the real 737 CDU. The font styling, image sharpness, and color reproduction all closely match what you would see on the real flight deck.

The CS 737X CDU v2 also features a handle, which on the real aircraft is used for the maintenance crew to remove the CDU. This isn’t entirely necessary in a home setup, but it is a nice touch.

The unit can be easily placed on a desk using the included desktop stand, or integrated directly into a larger cockpit setup.

The weight, rigidity, and metallic construction closely replicate the feel of the CDU we experienced in a 737 simulator. The silicone buttons also require a firm, deliberate press to actuate, helping prevent accidental double-inputs during turbulence. This tactile resistance closely matches the experience of using the real unit. Manually entering a long route, rather than importing it from SimBrief, will give your fingers a workout – and will give you a newfound appreciation for the import button.

For our testing inside of Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, we used the PMDG 737-800. We flew the following routes:

This allowed us to examine how the CS 737X CDU v2 handles routes of various duration.

For hardware, the device only requires a USB connection. It also requires the CockpitSimulator Bridge, which needs to be left open throughout the flight. This can be downloaded from the official Cockpit-Simulator site.

The overall feel of the unit, combined with the firm, deliberate key presses, adds another layer of immersion. More importantly, having a physical CDU means we can operate it directly — rather than panning the camera toward the virtual CDU, zooming in, and navigating it with a mouse. This makes interacting with the FMS considerably faster and more intuitive.

This is particularly useful when ATC gives you a direct-to instruction shortly after takeoff, while you are still hand-flying the aircraft. Performing the direct-to operation on a physical CDU is much easier than interacting with the virtual CDU, as it allows you to make the necessary inputs without taking your eyes away from the Primary Flight Display.

One of the first things that stood out was the extremely low input latency. Our key presses were reflected almost instantly on both the unit’s physical display and the virtual CDU inside Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, making the two feel effectively synchronized.

We were also able to switch seamlessly between the various CDU pages, even with longer flight plans loaded into the unit. Everything shown on the virtual CDU was accurately reproduced on the hardware, including aircraft-specific options for the PMDG 737-800 we were flying. The information was presented with accurate fonts, colors, and formatting, making the physical CDU feel like a natural extension of the one inside the simulator.

The CS 737X CDU v2 is the most premium and immersive Boeing 737 CDU we have tested. From the weight and feel of its metallic construction to the tactile resistance of the silicone keys and the accurate rendering of fonts and colors on the display, nearly every aspect of the unit contributes to an authentic experience. It's a fitting addition to any high-end home cockpit setup.

This level of construction and attention to detail comes at a price: the CS 737X CDU v2 retails for $799, which means it will likely be out of reach for many flight simmers. But if you're building a dedicated, high-end cockpit and looking for a CDU that closely replicates the experience of the real aircraft, it's an excellent addition.

#10524. Are school phone bans working so far? Here’s what early studies show

The argument for school cellphone bans is simple: Phones offer endless distraction. Take them away and students can focus on classwork, engage with peers and, ultimately, learn more.

But the reality is more complicated, as emerging research shows. Schools can lock phones away in pouches or banish them to backpacks, but they can’t shut out the digital world.

In the past few years, more than 40 U.S. states have passed laws that restrict cellphones at schools, according to the Phone Free Schools State Report Card, which tracks state phone legislation. But those laws vary widely and often let schools design their own policies, resulting in a patchwork of rules and enforcement across the country.

A large-scale study published Tuesday found strict cellphone restrictions — ones that require students to put phones in locked pouches for the entire school day — result in small academic gains. But, the researchers said, the gains can add up if schools continue banning phones.

Phone bans appear to help, to a point

The study, led by Harvard’s Center for Education Policy Research, found the schools with strict phone restrictions saw “modest” improvements in academic growth, compared with students in similar schools without those restrictions. The study, which analyzed test scores of 3.3 million students at 4,600 schools nationally, estimates the academic gains were equivalent to about an additional week or two of learning over a school year.

Student achievement has been falling globally since 2013, which is roughly when social media-enabled smartphones took off. The researchers sought to determine if the decline is being reversed now that schools have started taking phones away, said Harvard professor Thomas Kane, one of the study’s authors.

“Our answer is yes, phone bans do have a positive effect on growth. But it’s not a panacea,” Kane said. Learning loss was gradual over a decade, he notes, and it’s not surprising that gains would also be gradual. The study used math and reading test data for grades four through 10 from the past five academic years.

“While schools should not expect large boosts in achievement immediately, storing students’ phones seems to be a cost-effective way to add 1-2 weeks of instruction each year, which could add up over time, just as the initial declines did,” the study says.

The boost is equal to about half the annual decline in test scores since smartphones became mainstream, the study said.

Academic gains are overall ‘disappointing,’ one researcher says

Still, the connection between phones and learning is not clear-cut.

A different study published in May concluded strict school phone bans had “close to zero” effect on test scores. It compared schools with bans with tens of thousands of other schools.

The National Bureau of Economic Research study looked at a different set of standardized test scores than Harvard’s study, as well as GPS phone activity, teacher surveys and data from Yondr, the leading provider of lockable phone pouches, at 4,600 schools that use the pouches.

The study had found “modest positive effects” in high school test scores over three years, particularly in math. But the report’s authors, researchers at Stanford, the University of Michigan, Duke and the University of Pennsylvania, were hesitant to conclude overall learning benefits from the bans.

Both studies point to a similar conclusion, said Stanford education economist Thomas Dee, an author of the NBER study. “The early results from school phone bans are largely disappointing and raise unresolved questions,” Dee said.

Noting that the Harvard study showed learning gains may accumulate over time, Dee said: “I hope they’re right. However, I’m not comfortable making that extrapolation from estimates that are small, sensitive and based on just a few years of phone bans.”

The reasons, Dee said, could be that students are still distracted on other devices at school. Or, he said, “it may be that we see these disappointing results because out-of-school phone use is harming child development.”

Phones aren’t the only tech distracting teens

Just because schools or states have phone bans does not mean they’re being enforced, said Jean Twenge, a psychologist at San Diego State University and author of “10 Rules for Raising Kids in a High-Tech World.”

Ask any teacher — or teenager — and they’ll tell you that some phone bans are largely cosmetic. Teens come up with creative workarounds, including stowing burner phones or even phone-shaped rocks in their locked pouches. At schools that rely on students to keep phones in backpacks, adherence to the ban can be spotty.

“It happens pretty often that there’s a policy of no phones during the school day, bell-to-bell, and you go into the school and phones are everywhere,” Twenge said.

Even without phones, “Do they have laptops at school? Are they just doing social media on laptops instead?” Twenge said.

Phone use outside of school affects academics too, Twenge said. “If they have that phone available when they’re studying, how much are they really taking in?”

Kane, of the Harvard study, agrees the effect of cellphone use outside of school is “the big question.” But researchers have not been able to investigate parents and educators’ suspicions that late-night binges on YouTube and other platforms are costly for students.

“I find it astonishing that social media companies know how much time kids spend on their platforms, but that data has never been linked to student outcomes,” Kane said. “We can’t provide answers until the social media companies share data.”

—Jocelyn Gecker, AP Education Writer

Darrel Dai wants to know the exact reasons why Jensen resigned.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Just days after Jensen Huang suddenly resigned from his position at Nvidia, an Nvidia Robot Research Engineer said that he would leave the company as well. But more than just showing support for the former CEO with a generic “I stand with Jensen” message, Darrel Dai laid out several reasons for the decision on X.

I’ve decided to leave NVIDIA. There are a few things I want to say. As a robotics engineer at NVIDIA, I have seen Jensen as much more than the company’s CEO. I admire his willingness to invest in a future that was not yet obvious. He committed to CUDA long before the deep learning boom and positioned NVIDIA for AI before it became everyone’s priority. Those decisions helped build the infrastructure that powers today’s AI. I have seen that same vision in physical AI: investing in robotics, sharing open-source tools and projects, and building computing platforms that bring AI into the physical world. This is the work I do every day—and a future I believe in. But what matters most to me is the culture he helped build. Engineers are encouraged to explore, take risks, and learn from mistakes. Jensen reads employees’ Top 5 emails, follows their work, and engages directly. In a company this large, that connection matters. It makes an individual engineer feel that their ideas can still be heard. That is why this has been so disappointing. I do not have all the facts surrounding the allegations, and I cannot prejudge the investigation. My admiration for Jensen does not put him above scrutiny. What I find difficult to accept is having to come to terms with his departure before receiving an explanation that helps me understand it. What this means for our direction, our culture, and the people doing the work remains unclear to me. I have felt that engineers’ perspectives matter here. On this decision, I have not felt heard. That gap has been more painful than I expected. I understand that some information cannot be shared immediately. But that does not erase the feeling of being left outside a decision that affects the company we help build every day. A company’s greatness comes from its leadership, its governance, and the people who turn its ambitions into reality. Employees’ trust and sense of belonging are part of that, too. Jensen’s vision and the engineering culture he shaped were important reasons I wanted to stay. His departure led me to decide that my own chapter here should also come to a close. I leave with sadness and gratitude. The colleagues I have worked with, and the work we believed in together, will always matter to me. These are my personal views.November 15, 2026

“What I find difficult to accept is having to come to terms with his departure before receiving an explanation that helps me understand it. What this means for our direction, our culture, and the people doing the work remains unclear to me,” the engineer posted. “I have felt that engineers’ perspectives matter here. On this decision, I have not felt heard. That gap has been more painful than I expected.”

It seems that Jensen Huang has gained the respect of the people working under him, with many calling for his reinstatement despite the many controversies he is currently facing. There’s also an online petition demanding that the Nvidia board “Bring Jensen Back,” with over 150,000 signatures at the time of writing.

Nvidia is centered around Jensen Huang, with the former chief executive reportedly having a small army of 60 people directly reporting to him. But despite his busy schedule and legendary persona, Dai said that “Jensen reads employees’ Top 5 emails, follows their work, and engages directly,” and that “It makes an individual engineer feel that their ideas can still be heard.” Dai also pointed out that “employees’ trust and sense of belonging” are part of what makes a company great. More importantly, Nvidia is known as one of the tech companies with the most generous pay packages. Jensen was even quoted saying, “I pay my employees as much as I can.”

It remains unclear what the former Nvidia CEO will do after all these issues. Elon Musk has already said on X that “it would be an honor” to hire Jensen Huang, especially as he’s embarking on his own ambitious chipmaking journey. As for the employees left behind at Nvidia, some are staying and have shown their full support to interim CEO Colette Kress, while many more want him back. However, there has also been talk that various Silicon Valley tech and semiconductor firms are aggressively attempting to poach Nvidians, although these are just rumors so far.

#10520. Prompt Management in TypeScript: LangSmith vs Git vs 3 Open-Source Registries

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Every prompt registry we tested can change a prompt in a running TypeScript app, roll it back, and give production and staging different versions. LangSmith's prompt hub, Langfuse, Phoenix and AcruxCore all passed those three tests. The real differences show up elsewhere: which template syntax each one accepts, how many npm packages it pulls in, how long a change takes to reach the app, and what happens when the registry is down.

We tested all of this with one small app and one prompt, which has a condition and a loop. Git files served as the baseline. Every number below comes from a recorded run.

Most teams start with prompts in code: a template string, or a .txt file next to the code that uses it. That works until a product manager wants to change one sentence, and the change has to wait for a full release.

A prompt registry moves the text out of the deploy. The app fetches the prompt by name and by a label such as production. You change which version the label points to, and the app picks up the new text without a deploy.

LangSmith's prompt hub is the best-known registry, but it is not the only one. Several of the LangSmith alternatives also manage prompts, and three of them are open source and self-hostable: Langfuse, Phoenix and AcruxCore. We covered how those tools handle tracing in Self-Hosted LangSmith Alternatives: 4 Tools Tested on One TypeScript Agent. This article covers prompts only.

Every tool got the same prompt, support-reply. Its template takes three variables: a customer name, a plan, and a list of help articles. It has one condition: a priority line appears only for premium customers. It also has one loop: one line per help article. In Jinja2 syntax, the template looks like this:

One help article contains the text Settings > Export. We included it on purpose, to catch any tool that HTML-escapes > into >.

Every tool then ran the same sequence from a TypeScript script:

Each tool used its own documented TypeScript SDK. The four registries passed all six steps. The rest of this article covers how each one got there, and what it cost.

Keeping prompts in the repository costs almost nothing. The template sits in prompts/support-reply.njk, and nunjucks, the JavaScript port of Jinja2, renders it:

The autoescape: false line matters. Our first version called nunjucks.renderString() directly, and the test failed. The default environment HTML-escapes its output, so Settings > Export reached the model as Settings > Export. Escaping is correct for web pages and wrong for prompts.

Git gives you full Jinja2, code review on every prompt change, and history in the same place as the code. What it can't do is change a prompt in a running app. Every edit, and every rollback, waits for a deploy.

LangSmith stores a prompt as a serialized LangChain object (ChatPromptTemplate), not as plain text. LangSmith's own documentation says you must use the LangChain npm package to pull prompts in TypeScript (Manage prompts programmatically). So a plain TypeScript app that uses the openai package still needs langchain and @langchain/core:

Those three packages installed 23 packages and 70 MB. Most of the size is @langchain/* (27 MB) and js-tiktoken (22 MB).

Templates. In TypeScript, LangChain accepts f-string and mustache templates. Mustache sections ({{#docs}}…{{/docs}}) handled our loop. Mustache has no ==, though, so the premium check became an is_premium boolean computed in code. We also tried templateFormat: "jinja2", which LangChain's Python package supports. In TypeScript it threw DEFAULT_PARSER_MAPPING[templateFormat] is not a function.

Labels and rollback. production and staging are reserved tags, and the documentation moves them in the UI. The langsmith JavaScript client has no public method that moves a tag. Our script called the same REST route the SDK uses internally (POST /api/v1/repos/-//tags). It worked, but it is not a documented API.

Caching. The SDK caches prompts for 300 seconds by default. In our test, a running app saw the new version 300 seconds after we moved the tag.

Langfuse's TypeScript client is one package, @langfuse/client. It installed 5 packages and 8 MB:

Creating a version, moving a label and reading by label are all public SDK calls: prompt.create, prompt.update and prompt.get (Get started with prompt management).

Templates. The documentation shows only {{variable}} substitution. But compile() calls the mustache library, so sections worked for our loop. The type signature accepts only string values, so passing a list needed a cast. The Langfuse UI colours the section tags red, and it lists title and body as the prompt's variables, not docs or is_premium. We would not depend on behaviour the documentation doesn't promise. When we sent the Jinja2 version instead, Langfuse returned the {% if %} and {% for %} tags unchanged, with no error. The model would have received them as text.

Caching. The cache time is 60 seconds by default (Caching). Our app saw the change after 62 seconds. Langfuse is also the only client with a fallback option: a prompt string the SDK uses when it cannot reach the server on a cold start.

Phoenix's TypeScript client fetches a prompt by name and tag, and toSDK() converts it into the message format the openai package expects. Phoenix templates only replace variables, so the condition and the loop have to run in your code before rendering:

That is 16 lines, against 6 to 8 for the other registries. All the extra lines are template logic that now lives in the app.

Templates. Phoenix offers MUSTACHE, F_STRING and NONE formats (Prompts reference). Even in MUSTACHE mode, though, rendering is a plain replacement of {{name}}. When we sent mustache sections, they came back unchanged, with no error.

Errors. getPrompt() catches every error, logs it and returns null. You can see this in the client source, src/utils/getPromptBySelector.ts. A missing prompt and an unreachable server look the same to your code, which is why the snippet checks for null.

Size and caching. The client installed 57 packages and 90 MB. Most of that is OpenTelemetry, which comes in through its @arizeai/phoenix-otel dependency. The client has no prompt cache, so every render is a network call. That is also why a label change showed up immediately: 0 seconds in our test.

AcruxCore stores Jinja2 templates and renders them on the server with nunjucks. The SDK sends the variables and gets back finished messages:

The template from the test section works as it is, condition and loop included, with no is_premium flag computed in code. A label is called an alias here, and promoteAlias() moves it (Manage prompts via the SDK). The SDK installed 3 packages and 12 MB. Most of the 12 MB is one OpenTelemetry package, @opentelemetry/semantic-conventions.

Templates. Jinja2 only. When we committed the mustache version, AcruxCore rejected it at commit time with Template parse error: unexpected token: #. That is a clear error, but it also means that moving mustache prompts from LangSmith or Langfuse requires rewriting them.

We sent the same two templates, a Jinja2 one and a mustache one, to each tool's own renderer:

The rows that matter most are the ones where the tags were left in the output, because those failures produce no error. The model receives raw template syntax, and the only symptom is a strange answer. Whatever tool you pick, test one prompt with logic in it before you move the rest.

Putting logic in the template is not automatically better. It lets someone change the condition without a deploy. It also lets them break the condition without a deploy. Keeping logic in code, as Phoenix forces you to do, puts every branch under code review and in your tests.

A registry is a new runtime dependency, so we tested an outage. The app reached each registry through a local proxy, and we switched the proxy off. A separate process then started while the registry was still unreachable.

LangSmith, Langfuse and AcruxCore keep serving the last good version while the registry is down, even after the cache time has passed. The risk is a cold start: a new container or a serverless function that boots during the outage. Langfuse's fallback option is the built-in answer to that. With the other tools, keep a copy of each prompt in your code as a fallback, which brings back part of the Git setup.

Keep prompts in Git if engineers make every prompt change and your deploys are quick. Set autoescape: false, and you get Jinja2, reviews and history for free.

Use LangSmith's prompt hub if you already use LangChain, or already trace with LangSmith. If your app doesn't use LangChain, budget for the extra dependency and for the tag moves that only the UI supports.

Use Langfuse if you want a small client, a local compile(), and a fallback for cold starts. Keep to {{variable}} substitution unless you are comfortable relying on mustache behaviour that the documentation doesn't promise.

Use Phoenix if you already use it for tracing, or if you prefer all template logic in code. Remember the null check, and that every render is a network call.

Use AcruxCore if you want real conditions and loops in the template and rendering on the server. Expect one network call per new set of variables, and a personal API key for writes.

Before you choose, run one of your own prompts with real logic in it through the tool's SDK, not through its playground. Two of the four registries we tested failed on template syntax without any error, and an SDK run is where you would see that.

Kit that any PC builder or hobbyist will love

It's fun to build a PC. This is Tom's Hardware, after all. While the AI boom has forced prices to go up and up, there's still a lot of fun to be had putting a build together. Researching your parts, weighing up the pros and cons, then putting it all together. Seeing your brand new PC pass its first boot test, waiting to see if it'll actually load and not just beep and stay blank, is always a thrill.

To get to that point, though, you're going to need some kit. You'll need tools to build, but also to maintain, clean, and repair: your PC is going to need it all at some stage. I've built my own toolkit over the years. My go-to right now is a Hoto screwdriver, but I've got electric dusters, flashlights, screw kits, the lot, all ready for a project or two. My toolkit is versatile enough that it's helped me just as much while I renovate my home as it has in putting together my last build.

● Check out all the PC tool deals on Amazon

My toolkit is pretty expansive these days, but if you or a loved one is just starting out, you'll probably be wondering what to buy. I've put together a mix of the must-buys and nice-to-haves below for any PC builder, maker, and hobbyist's toolkit to help you decide.

If you're not a hobbyist yourself, these tools would make great gifts to share over the holiday season, too!

Here's some of the kit that we'd recommend you buy to get started.

With USB Type-C charging, six brightness modes, and a magnetic base, the Wuben E7 is a useful flashlight for makers and tinkerers who want extra light for their work, without compromising on quality.

Cleaning is one of those PC maintenance tasks that we've all probably left until our PC cases are fill with dust and grime, not to mention our keyboards and mice. A good set of cleaning tools, especially an air duster, can make all the difference. These tools are versatile, so you can use them whenever you need to defeat some dust and grime, whether it's your car dashboard or your project room.

Designed for electronics, these four, 10oz bottle of compressed air will blow the dust, dead skin and last week's sandwich from your keyboard and help prevent the inside of your PC case becoming a biohazard.

A brush is an underrated part of any toolkit. You've got every type of brush you'll need included in this kit to deep clean your PC, keyboard and whatever else needs cleaning in your rig.

You'll want Isopropyl Alcohol on hand as it's safe to use with electronics. Buying in bulk and decanting into dollar store spray bottles is the smart way to use it, from a cost point of view.

This isn't an exhaustive list, but a good selection of the tools and accessories that I reckon every PC builder, maker, and hobbyist needs at their disposal.

You won't always need them. Some of them aren't glamorous or exciting, but they'll all indispensable parts of your toolkit that, once you've got them close to hand, you'll come to rely on them.

#10515. With The Blood Of Dawnwalker’s New Game+ Mode, It’s Worth Going Back To See How Much You Can Get Done

The Blood of Dawnwalker‘s latest patch 1.2 is now live, adding a new game+ mode which increases the level cap from 50 to 100 and, perhaps most interestingly, removes zone scaling. In the original game, protagonist Coen could, in a bit of player-guided misadventure, stumble into a zone he was wholly underleveled for and get his shit rocked by a pack of wild boars or the errant bear. That possibility added an extra dash of tension to a game already fraught with time pressure and some tough decision-making, and I’d be curious to see what the game feels like without that added bit of danger.

New game+ comes after developer Rebel Wolves added a bunch of extra bells and whistles to the game post-launch including a new difficulty tier that introduced additional combat assists for those having an issue with the game’s directional parry system. Speaking of, the devs also bolted its directional parry system onto your ability to pet the various cats Coen can encounter, letting you stroke them this way and that because why not?

Dawnwalker‘s new game+ mode might go on my list of odds and ends to try before the end of the year. The massively increased level cap is appealing just for the prospect of seeing exactly how chonky the boars can get now that they scale to my level. The game’s time management system gives you ample opportunity to get the biggest quests done, but not everything can be completed in the 30 days you’re given to save your family.Â  I’m curious to see just how much you actually can get done, both within the time allotted and after everything’s over.

The original definition of "hacking" was making hardware and software do something it wasn't supposed to.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Hacking stories these days mostly involve someone using an army of AI agents to find vulnerabilities in networks and software that were carefully hidden in plain sight. Today, for a change, we have a story about hacking in its original meaning — twisting computing artifacts into purposes not in their design spec. David Oberhollenzer, aka Goliath, a greybeard in spirit if not in shade, crafted a 100% valid ZIP file that's simultaneously an archive, BIOS-bootable, and a Multiboot-compatible OS image.

You can unpack the ZIP file just like any other, boot it using Linux's GRUB, QEMU, or any other Multiboot-compatible loader (even if imaged to different media), or alternatively, perform the finest party trick: image-write it to a floppy and boot from it directly from BIOS on any compatible PC, without modification.

Much like me, that sequence of words may be triggering a head-tilt reminiscent of a confused puppy, so we'll explain. The first thing you need to know is that unlike most file types, the metadata (in this case, file directory) of a ZIP is actually at the end of the archive. Up to that point, the data is comprised of every compressed file in sequence.

The file packs all have a predictable structure: "PK" followed by bytes 03 04, metadata (including name), some extra/comment fields, and then the file's contents. Notably, any file can be stored uncompressed, and Goliath made use of that for the very first file, called ZIPHEAD.COM — remember, this is the start of the ZIP archive.

Goliath said that it was "easy" to make the ZIP file a valid Multiboot system image. A valid image only needs to contain bytes 0x1BADB002 in the first 8 KiB, followed by some flags and a checksum. It was trivial to place that datum in ZIPHEAD's data, along with the location of where the bootloader lies.

Grub or QEMU don't care about anything else in the image, as once they have the initialization information, from that point it's the bootloader's problem. The actual bootloader, predictably, is in ZIPHEAD's uncompressed data, and the image will happily boot directly, or, say, from a floppy.

Making the same exact archive bootable via a standard PC BIOS took a little more work and some clever shenanigans. Making a disk bootable is simple enough: the BIOS reads the first exact 512 bytes of the disk's contents, and if they end with bytes 0x55AA, then it's bootable, and the BIOS starts executing whatever code is the first byte.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Placing 0x55AA precisely at position 510 of the ZIP, already in ZIPHEAD's contents, is once again simple, and won't corrupt the Multiboot image, as if you'll recall, the Multiboot spec is flexible with data locations. But you may wonder: once the BIOS runs code in sequence starting from the ZIP's first byte, then ZIPHEAD's header ("PK" + 0x0304, plus all metadata) surely is garbage for practical purposes, and not proper code? Well, yes, but actually no.

The first four bytes represent CPU instructions that don't write anything to memory, so they're harmless, other than a push-to-stack. The next few belong to ZIPHEAD's metadata, and Goliath massaged those values to represent instructions that would either be innocuous or perform operations he could use, namely using the modification time bytes as instructions to jump further down the data.

Sounds simple, but the actual process of choosing bytes that represent (1) non-crashy CPU instructions, (2) useful code for setting up the boot process, and (3) still represent a valid file header in a ZIP archive is far trickier than the above. Do go and check out the full blog post if you want all the details.

#10512. Technical Aspects of AI-Generated Video Assets for Web Design

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI-generated videos are becoming an important part of modern web design. Designers can now create animated backgrounds, product demonstrations, hero section videos, and visual storytelling elements without relying entirely on traditional video production. However, generating a visually appealing video is only one part of the process. To use AI-generated videos effectively on a website, developers and designers must also understand video formats, visual quality, file optimization, and website performance.

These technical factors directly influence how videos appear across devices, how quickly pages load, and how smoothly visitors interact with a website.

Video format selection is one of the first technical decisions when preparing AI-generated assets for the web. Different formats offer different levels of compression, compatibility, and visual quality.

For most websites, MP4 with H.264 remains a dependable default. WebM or AV1 can be offered as additional formats where appropriate.

Developers should also consider browser compatibility before selecting a format. Providing multiple sources allows browsers to choose a supported option.

AI-generated videos can sometimes contain visual inconsistencies, unnatural movements, distorted objects, or changes in lighting between frames. These issues become more noticeable when videos are displayed in large website sections.

Resolution is an important factor in maintaining visual quality. Common resolutions include:

However, higher resolution does not automatically mean better website performance or user experience. A 4K video may look impressive, but loading it unnecessarily can increase bandwidth consumption.

Frame rate also affects the viewing experience. Many website videos work well at 24 or 30 frames per second. Higher frame rates may be useful for fast-moving scenes, but they also increase the amount of visual data that needs to be processed.

Designers should review AI-generated footage before publishing it. Checking transitions, motion consistency, sharpness, and color accuracy helps prevent distracting visual problems.

Large video files can significantly increase website loading times. This is especially important for websites with video backgrounds, animated landing pages, and multiple visual sections.

Video optimization involves reducing file size without making the footage noticeably worse.

Some practical optimization techniques include:

Compression: Video compression reduces unnecessary data while preserving important visual details. Developers can use encoding tools such as FFmpeg to adjust bitrate, resolution, and codec settings.

Bitrate control: Bitrate determines how much data is used to represent each second of video. A higher bitrate generally preserves more detail but increases file size. Selecting an appropriate bitrate depends on the video's resolution, movement, and intended display size.

Trimming unnecessary footage: Website videos rarely need to be several minutes long. Removing unused sections helps reduce file size and keeps visual content focused.

Removing unnecessary audio: Background videos that do not require sound should be exported without an audio track. This reduces unnecessary data and supports a cleaner user experience.

Responsive video delivery: Websites should serve appropriately sized assets for different screen sizes. A smaller video may be sufficient for mobile users, while desktop visitors can receive a higher-resolution version.

These techniques help developers balance visual quality with efficient content delivery.

Even a well-optimized video can affect website performance if it is implemented incorrectly. Developers should consider how videos are loaded, displayed, and processed by browsers.

For example, automatically loading several large videos when a page opens can consume significant bandwidth. Instead, developers can use lazy loading strategies for videos that appear further down the page.

For background videos, the HTML video element offers several useful attributes:

Developers should also avoid autoplaying large videos unnecessarily. A static image can often provide a better experience on mobile devices or slower connections.

Performance testing tools such as Google Lighthouse and Chrome DevTools can help identify whether video assets are affecting loading speed, bandwidth usage, or rendering performance.

Technical optimization should not come at the expense of accessibility. Background videos should not distract users or make website content difficult to understand.

Developers should respect the prefers-reduced-motion media query, which allows users who prefer reduced animation to receive a less motion-intensive experience.

A suitable static background image can be displayed as an alternative.

Mobile compatibility is equally important. Smaller screens, limited data plans, and varying network conditions can make heavy video assets less practical. Testing videos on different devices and connection speeds helps identify potential problems before publication.

AI-generated video assets offer exciting possibilities for modern web design, but their successful implementation requires more than creative output. Choosing suitable video formats, maintaining consistent visual quality, compressing files, and considering website performance are all essential parts of the development process.

By combining thoughtful video production with responsive delivery, accessibility considerations, and performance testing, designers and developers can create engaging websites without compromising loading speed or usability. As AI video technology continues to evolve, understanding these technical fundamentals will remain valuable for building efficient and visually appealing web experiences.

Doom now runs on a USB flash drive’s built-in LCD and is played by copying files to and from it, as hardware hacker Aaron Christophel showed in a teardown video. The marking on the drive’s display chip had been removed, but an open debug port let him extract its firmware, which enabled identification. He was then able to use AI to reverse-engineer the hardware and get the game running on the drive’s screen.

The off-the-shelf drive, the MOVESPEED MSSU10, has USB-A on one end and USB-C on the other, and the 128GB model, the smallest capacity in the range, cost him about 50 euros. Its screen normally shows status data such as transfer speed, how full the drive is, and its temperature.

The main flash controller is the Silicon Motion SM2320G, one we have reviewed in portable SSDs like the Kingston XS2000 and Lexar SL660 Blaze, with a separate C*Core CCM4101 microcontroller — which has 2MB of flash and a small amount of RAM to itself — for the 428 x 142 color LCD. The NAND carries SanDisk markings. All of this is fairly standard portable SSD hardware, aside from the display.

The drive’s metal body uses heavily glued plastic end pieces but, past that, the display lifts off first and unplugs. The board slides out after the USB-C end cap is removed, in this case with minor cosmetic damage inflicted. The display chip’s marking is scrubbed, most likely with a laser, by the hacker’s reckoning, which can hinder identification and tinkering. Luckily, a probe on the debug pads, ground, and a 3.3V pin connected on the first try, and memory was immediately readable.

The bootloader returned a version string dated 2023, followed by the full firmware, which helped greatly with identification. He says the chip is marketed as one for security — for fingerprint readers and access control, for example — but no related features were found to be enabled for this drive. He also discovered that, although the data sheet and stock firmware declare a 200 MHz operating clock frequency, it measured 40.2 MHz. This is unexplained.

One critical issue is immediately apparent: how do you play on a drive with no buttons? The display chip has no USB connection of its own and, from the connected PC or host, it only sees the storage controller’s activity, which it uses to gauge transfer speed. The primary storage controller has read and write counters, and the chip pulls these every 50 ms over I2C. Christophel says this is far easier than relying on a single physical button, as he did on a previous power bank mod.

The solution, then, is a PC script, doomctl.py, which turns key presses into small, timed transfers in each direction. The commands are simply encoded as transfer rates, at five levels per direction, and each read/write pair can map to a certain button combination. Arrow keys are for movement and turning, Space or Ctrl for firing and opening doors, and M for the menu, keeping it simple. Ordinary copying, without the script, can still steer, but the control scheme is much nicer.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Performance is…well, not really playable at about 13 frames per second, although the game logic runs at Doom’s normal 35 ticks per second. This is why he names the chip’s clock as the biggest potential performance gain. The game itself is built on DMC100-DOOM, Artur Bieniek’s port for very small microcontrollers. Only the first map, E1M1, fits in the chip’s flash, and no sound is produced as the drive lacks a buzzer. Christophel did play the level end to end, noting the low resolution.

AI did the heavy lifting: the reverse engineering as well as the port, and Christophel said, “I would not be able to do such a thing in a few hours.”

The open-source project, with its code and prebuilt firmware published, is likely to draw attention and may spawn similar hacks. The tools required are relatively minimal, mainly a debug probe, and he does suggest backing up the stock firmware before trying. For his own unit, he put it back together to use as a normal drive, but one that can still play Doom, if so desired.

All Elite Wrestling's recent Full Gear event had no shortage of great moments, but Austin Creed stole the show with a move straight out of Street Fighter. After teaming up with his Next Level partner Kofi Kingston and Swerve Strickland to take on Bandido, Hangman Adam Page, and Brody King in a Texas Death Match, anything went in this brawl — including vintage NES accessories.

Looking the worse for wear at King's hands, Creed busted out an NES Power Glove and landed a Shoryuken uppercut that exploded in a shower of sparks, knocking his burly foe flat on his back. In another video game crossover, former WWE champion Cody Rhodes played Guile in the live-action Street Fighter movie, which was released last month, and he even cosplayed as the character at WWE SummerSlam. Without a doubt, Nvidia's dominance in the AI hardware market stems not only from the capabilities of its AI accelerators and its vast software ecosystem, but also from its aggressive procurement strategy that effectively denies its rivals access to sufficient production capacity at TSMC and other contractors. The result of his deals is that supply and capacity commitments rose by almost a quarter of a trillion dollars in a single quarter, primarily due to memory procurement, according to SemiAnalysis. However, even Nvidia's former chief executive Jensen Huang had apparently begun to question the sustainability of this strategy before his departure, based on reports from The Wall Street Journal and SemiAnalysis.

Over the past several years, Nvidia has not only captured the vast majority of the AI accelerator market, but has also secured a substantial proportion of the world's production capacity for advanced logic, high-bandwidth memory (HBM), and various other components required to build AI accelerators and systems, which has limited the ability of its competitors to ramp up shipments of their processors. To support the deals, Jensen Huang personally negotiated agreements with major suppliers in Taiwan and South Korea.

The massive scale of Nvidia's procurement commitments also enabled the company to secure more favorable quotes than its rivals. SemiAnalysis estimates that SK hynix could charge Nvidia between $3.00 and $3.30 per gigabit of HBM4 memory in 2027, whereas other first-tier customers, such as AMD, Amazon, Broadcom, and Google, would pay between $3.70 and $4.10 per gigabit. The analysts believe that as part of an informal arrangement between the two companies, Nvidia gives SK Group preferential access to its AI GPUs.

While Nvidia's ability to secure vast production capacities has been instrumental in its success, such commitments also carry considerable risks. At a meeting with senior executives in August, Huang reportedly expressed concerns about the massive volumes of wafers and memory that Nvidia had committed to purchase as major cloud service providers sought to reduce their reliance on the company's hardware in favor of alternative AI accelerator platforms, according to The Wall Street Journal.

In a bid to diversify its customer base and create additional demand for its products, Nvidia offered financial guarantees to emerging cloud service providers and data center developers that otherwise could not afford to procure its hardware at scale. As of the end of its fiscal second quarter, Nvidia had $530 billion in gross off-balance-sheet guarantees, up from $184 billion a quarter earlier, as well as $99 billion worth of equity investments, according to SemiAnalysis. As half a trillion dollars seems gargantuan, here is a breakdown based on a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission:

The scale of such commitments raised concerns even within Nvidia. Then-CFO Colette Kress questioned the criteria used to select recipients of financial support and the potential returns on such arrangements. She also reportedly reduced Nvidia's initial financial commitment to OpenAI's massive data center project in Ohio by half before the two companies signed an agreement on August 17. The facility is expected to house some $300 billion worth of Nvidia processors.

At some point, Huang himself began to question the merits of Nvidia's aggressive financing strategy in the event of his departure, essentially calling the current interim CEO, Colette Kress, a mere 'reporting CFO' rather than an executive capable of making strategic decisions. He also expressed concerns about massive wafer and memory procurement commitments as major cloud service providers sought to reduce their reliance on Nvidia’s GPUs.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Despite questionable commitments, without Huang and his personal relationships with executives at major semiconductor companies, Nvidia may find it harder to secure preferential treatment from its suppliers. SemiAnalysis believes that customers other than Nvidia could account for over 70% of TSMC production capacity in 2028. While this could enable Nvidia’s competitors to significantly increase shipments of their AI processors, it could also affect the willingness of Taiwanese and South Korean suppliers to invest aggressively in additional production capacity without the kind of assurances that Huang used to provide.

#10507. GTA 6 Has A Lot Of Different Bird Species, Here’s How Many

Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 has a lot of details and depth, including dozens of different bird species for people to find. If you're a birder, you're in for a good time.

According to The Guardian, Rockstar confirmed that there are 62 types of birds that players can spot. Players can whip out binoculars to "study" birds and animals like they could in Rockstar's last game, Red Dead Redemption II.

As PC Gamer reminds us, Florida is home to more than 500 bird types, so GTA 6 will have just a fraction of the different kinds of birds people can find in real Florida. GTA 6 was never going to replicate every single bird, of course.

Some of the birds that are found in Florida, and probably GTA 6 as well, include flamingoes, spoonbills, wood storks, egrets, kites, terns, and scrub jays. Florida is also home to bald eagles, and we'd expect them to show up in GTA 6.

Inclusive of birds, GTA 6 has more than 170 animal types, including cane toads, alligators, manatees, and rhesus macaque monkeys.

GTA 6 launches on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S. The game launches at midnight local time, so it will be playable for people in New Zealand and Australia very soon. You can switch your Xbox region to New Zealand to play early, if that works.

#10505. Nintendo Switch 2 emulation on Android already has The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake up and running

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake now runs surprisingly well on phones after just a week of additional emulator development.

Legend of Zelda fans all over the world have been marveling at the Ocarina of Time remake’s visuals and enhanced gameplay systems on the Nintendo Switch 2, but the Android emulator scene has been busy marveling over something just a little bit different. One Redditor got the latest Zelda game running on Banana Native, a free emulator that’s available right now on GitHub.

Ocarina of Time remake performance has now reached a major milestone into the 30 FPS territory with frame gen, which means the game is actually running at around 15 FPS, but then scaled and interpolated using AI frame generation to appear like 30 FPS. Banana Native isn’t a traditional emulator, as it doesn’t emulate hardware. Rather, it uses the game’s own ARM64 code to run on the phone’s CPU. The Switch 2 is powered by a mobile Nvidia chip, after all.

The user is running the Ocarina of Time remake on a Poco F7 Ultra, which sports a two-generation-old Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite (Gen 4) processor. The latest phones that are coming out, like the Redmagic 12 Pro, run a 6th-gen Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme chip, so performance could be a lot better on a newer phone. Apps like Banana Native require specific driver support for each phone to run, and as I pointed out in my Redmagic 12 Pro review, platforms like Droid Deck and Game Native don’t yet have proper drivers for the newest chips.

9to5Google’s Damien Wilde recently reviewed Droid Deck, another native-type emulator that lets you legally play Steam games you own on your phone by just signing into your Steam account. It works extremely well on lots of Android phones and helps showcase just how far Android emulation has come this year.
